beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about Retrieval-Augmented Generation, giving an AI model a search step so it can look things up instead of guessing, and three questions that catch the difference between an answer that's actually grounded in what it found, and one that just sounds like it is.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01.

beats.narration_text: Picture a support assistant that searches your company's policy documents before answering. It finds a real document. It quotes a real policy number. And the answer is still wrong, because the document it found was replaced eight months ago, and nobody told the search index.
beats.new_visual_element: A chat-style Q&A, a retrieved document card stamped with an old date, a confident answer bubble

shot.note: Generic/hypothetical scenario — no real product or vendor named, per FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: Here's the check, before any example: three questions, every time a retrieval-based answer shows up. One, Relevant: does the retrieved document actually address this question, or just share some keywords with it? Two, Current: is this the newest version, or a stale copy the index never updated? Three, Grounded: is the answer actually built from what was retrieved, or did the model fall back on what it already knew and just cite the document anyway?
beats.new_visual_element: Rubric card, all 3 questions shown together (Relevant / Current / Grounded)

shot.note: Framework shown fully before any example, matching prior STEM videos' rubric beat.

beats.narration_text: Back to that support bot. Relevant, yes, it's the right policy document. Current, no, it's eight months stale. Grounded, doesn't matter, because the document itself is wrong, so a technically-grounded answer is still a wrong answer. Retrieval didn't fail here. Freshness did.
beats.new_visual_element: The retrieved document (dated, visibly stale) shown side by side with the model's answer, both the document's date and the current date visible together

shot.note: Document date and current date both legible together — the mismatch is the visual point.

beats.narration_text: Now the case where retrieval is exactly the fix. Ask a model about an internal product that launched last week, with no retrieval, it has never seen that word and will either say so, or invent something plausible-sounding and wrong. Give it the actual internal launch doc, and now there's real, current, relevant text to ground the answer in. Same mechanism. Completely different outcome, because this time the source is actually right.
beats.new_visual_element: A 'no retrieval' attempt (invented, wrong answer) next to a 'with retrieval' attempt (correct, grounded in a current real document), both visibly labeled

shot.note: Stress-tests the rubric — retrieval alone isn't the fix; a genuinely relevant, current source is. Fair comparison (same mechanism, different source quality), not a strawman.

beats.narration_text: Here's something to check today. Take one answer your RAG system gave recently. Ask the three questions: was the source actually relevant, was it actually current, and can you point to the exact sentence the answer came from. If you can't point to that sentence, you don't know if it's grounded, you're just hoping.
beats.new_visual_element: The 3 questions restated as a checklist card

shot.note: Concrete action, distinct from B03's framework card.

beats.narration_text: Giving a model a search step doesn't make it honest. It makes it capable of being honest, only if what it finds is actually right, and it actually uses it.
